prompt: Which part of federal law contains the Hazardous Materials Regulations (HMR)?
choices: 49 CFR Parts 390-399
49 CFR Part 383
49 CFR Part 393
49 CFR Parts 171-180
explanation: The Hazardous Materials Regulations are found in Title 49 of the Code of Federal Regulations, Parts 171-180. Parts 390-399 are the general motor carrier safety rules, and Part 383 covers CDL standards.

prompt: At a minimum, how often must hazardous materials employees, including drivers, be trained and tested?
choices: Once a year, before the busy season
Once every three years
Once every two years
Once every five years
explanation: The regulations require hazmat employees to be trained and tested at least once every three years. The employer or its designated representative provides this training.

prompt: Rules that tell shippers how to package hazmat and drivers how to load, transport and unload it are called:
choices: Containment rules
Segregation rules
Routing rules
Communication rules
explanation: The regulations that keep the material contained (packaging, loading, transporting, unloading) are called containment rules. Labels, shipping papers and placards are used to communicate the risk.

prompt: Shippers put warning labels on packages and supply shipping papers and placards mainly in order to:
choices: Keep the material from leaking during a crash
Show which carrier owns the load
Communicate the risk of the material
Tell the driver which route to take
explanation: Labels, shipping papers, emergency response information and placards communicate the hazard to the shipper, the carrier and the driver. Shipping papers also let police and firefighters identify the hazard after a crash.

prompt: Who decides a hazardous material's identification number, proper shipping name, hazard class and packing group?
choices: The carrier's dispatcher
The shipper
The driver
The consignee
explanation: The shipper uses the hazardous materials regulations to determine the product's ID number, proper shipping name, hazard class, packing group, packaging, labels, markings and placards.

prompt: Before transport, which party checks that the shipper correctly described, marked and labeled a shipment, and refuses improper shipments?
choices: The National Response Center
The packaging manufacturer
The carrier
The consignee
explanation: The carrier takes the shipment to its destination. Before transport it checks that the shipper prepared the shipment correctly and refuses improper shipments.

prompt: A shipper offers you a drum of hazardous material that is slowly leaking. What should you do?
choices: Accept it and seal the leak with tape
Accept it if the vehicle is placarded
Accept it and report the leak at delivery
Refuse the package
explanation: Drivers must refuse leaking packages and shipments. It is illegal to move a vehicle with leaking hazardous materials.

prompt: How many hazard classes are used to classify hazardous materials?
explanation: There are nine hazard classes. Some classes are divided into divisions, such as 1.1 through 1.6 for explosives.

prompt: Hazard Class 3 is made up of:
choices: Flammable solids
Flammable liquids
Flammable and non-flammable gases
Oxidizers
explanation: Class 3 is flammable liquids, such as gasoline. Flammable gases are Division 2.1, flammable solids are Division 4.1, and oxidizers are Division 5.1.

prompt: Which hazard division is poisonous (toxic) gases?
choices: Division 2.3
Division 6.1
Division 2.2
Division 2.1
explanation: Division 2.3 is poisonous/toxic gases. Division 2.1 is flammable gases, 2.2 is non-flammable gases, and 6.1 is poison (toxic) material that is not a gas.

prompt: Battery fluid is an example of which hazard class?
choices: Class 7, Radioactive
Class 9, Miscellaneous
Class 5, Oxidizers
Class 8, Corrosives
explanation: Class 8 is corrosives; battery fluid is the manual's example.

prompt: Uranium belongs to which hazard class?
choices: Class 9
Class 6
Class 7
Class 1
explanation: Class 7 is radioactive material, such as uranium.

prompt: Division 4.3 materials are described as:
choices: Flammable solids
Spontaneously combustible
Organic peroxides
Dangerous when wet
explanation: Division 4.3 is dangerous when wet (sodium is an example). Division 4.1 is flammable solids and 4.2 is spontaneously combustible.

prompt: Which explosives division has a mass explosion hazard?
choices: Division 1.4
Division 1.3
Division 1.1
Division 1.2
explanation: Division 1.1 is mass explosion hazard (dynamite is the example). Division 1.2 is a projection hazard, 1.3 a fire hazard and 1.4 a minor explosion hazard.

prompt: Propane is classified as:
choices: Division 2.1, flammable gas
Class 3, flammable liquid
Division 2.3, poisonous gas
Division 2.2, non-flammable gas
explanation: Propane is the manual's example of a Division 2.1 flammable gas. Helium is the example of a non-flammable gas (2.2).

prompt: Infectious substances, such as a shipment of a disease-causing virus, are in which division?
choices: Division 6.1
Division 6.2
Class 9
Division 2.3
explanation: Division 6.2 is infectious substances. Division 6.1 is poison (toxic) material, such as potassium cyanide.

prompt: Fuel oil is an example of which category of hazardous material?
choices: Division 2.2 non-flammable gas
Class 9 miscellaneous material
Combustible liquid
Division 4.2 spontaneously combustible
explanation: Fuel oil is listed as a combustible liquid, a category outside the nine numbered classes. Gasoline, by contrast, is a Class 3 flammable liquid.

prompt: Which of these is considered a shipping paper?
choices: A bill of lading
An annual inspection report
A vehicle registration card
A driver's record of duty status
explanation: Shipping orders, bills of lading and manifests are all shipping papers. They describe the hazardous materials being transported.

prompt: How should you set hazmat shipping papers apart from other shipping papers?
choices: Keep them at the bottom of the stack
Tab them or keep them on top of the stack
Staple them to the back of the logbook
Store them in a separate folder in the sleeper
explanation: Hazmat shipping papers must be easy to recognize. Tab them or keep them on top of other shipping papers so they can be found quickly after a crash.

prompt: Where must the emergency response information for a hazmat load be kept?
choices: With the receiver's paperwork
At the carrier's terminal
In the trailer, next to the hazardous cargo
In the same place as the shipping paper
explanation: Emergency response information must be kept in the same location as the hazmat shipping paper.

prompt: On a shipping paper listing both hazardous and non-hazardous items, what may be placed in the "HM" column to mark a hazmat entry?
choices: A check mark
The letter H
An X
An asterisk
explanation: Hazmat entries must be listed first, highlighted in a contrasting color, or marked with an X in a column captioned HM. RQ may be used instead of X for a reportable quantity.

prompt: In what order does the basic description of a hazardous material appear on the shipping paper?
choices: Proper shipping name, hazard class, ID number, packing group
Hazard class, ID number, packing group, proper shipping name
Packing group, hazard class, proper shipping name, ID number
ID number, proper shipping name, hazard class, packing group
explanation: The basic description lists the identification number, proper shipping name, hazard class or division, and packing group (if any), in that order. For example: UN1263, Paint, 3, PG II.

prompt: A material in the Hazardous Materials Table has a "G" in Column 1. What must the shipping paper also show?
choices: The technical name of the hazardous material
The name and address of the packaging manufacturer
A second emergency phone number
The quantity in gallons only
explanation: G means the entry is a generic shipping name. A generic name must be accompanied by a technical name, which is the specific chemical that makes the product hazardous.

prompt: How must the shipper of a hazardous waste show that it is waste on the shipping paper?
choices: Write HW at the end of the description
Put WASTE before the proper shipping name
Use a red highlighter on the whole entry
Add the letters HW after the hazard class number
explanation: The shipper puts WASTE before the proper shipping name, for example: UN1090, Waste Acetone, 3, PG II.

prompt: Which of these must the emergency response information for a hazmat load include?
choices: The driver's medical card number
Immediate methods for handling fires
The vehicle's annual inspection date
The shipper's tax ID number
explanation: At a minimum it must include the basic description and technical name, immediate health hazards, fire or explosion risks, immediate precautions, methods for handling fires, initial methods for spills or leaks, and first aid measures.

prompt: How long must a shipper keep a copy of an ordinary (non-waste) hazmat shipping paper?
choices: 90 days after delivery
1 year after delivery
3 years after the material is delivered to the receiver
2 years after the first carrier accepts it
explanation: Shippers keep shipping papers (or an electronic image) for 2 years after the initial carrier accepts the material, or 3 years for hazardous waste.

prompt: In which case is a signed shipper's certification NOT required on the original shipping paper?
choices: The shipment will travel less than 100 miles on public roads
The load weighs less than 1,001 pounds
A private carrier is hauling its own product
The driver has a hazmat endorsement
explanation: The only exceptions are a private carrier transporting its own product and a package provided by the carrier, such as a cargo tank.

prompt: Which of these is a clue that a shipment may contain hazardous materials?
choices: The shipper is a pest control or agricultural supplier
The packages are heavy for their size
The load must be delivered early the next morning to a warehouse
The freight is stacked on wooden pallets
explanation: Clues include the shipper's business (paint dealer, chemical supply, pest control, agricultural supplier, explosives or fireworks dealer), placarded tanks, cylinders and drums, and labels or ID numbers on packages.

prompt: When hauling hazardous waste, what document must you sign by hand and carry?
choices: The Hazardous Materials Table
The Emergency Response Guidebook
A copy of 49 CFR Part 397
The Uniform Hazardous Waste Manifest
explanation: Hazardous waste travels with a Uniform Hazardous Waste Manifest. Each carrier must sign it by hand, and it is treated as a shipping paper.

prompt: Before hauling a material, you check three lists. Which list is Appendix B to 49 CFR 172.101?
choices: The List of Marine Pollutants
The List of Hazardous Substances and Reportable Quantities
The list of Table 1 placards
The list of forbidden materials
explanation: The three lists are the Hazardous Materials Table (172.101), Appendix A (Hazardous Substances and Reportable Quantities) and Appendix B (Marine Pollutants).

prompt: What do the letters RQ on a shipping paper mean?
choices: Required quarantine
Reduced quantity
Reportable quantity
Restricted quantity
explanation: RQ means the material is a hazardous substance being shipped in a reportable quantity or more in one package. It may appear before or after the basic description.

prompt: In the Hazardous Materials Table, what does a "Forbidden" entry in Column 3 mean?
choices: It may be hauled only with a special state permit
The material must never be transported
It needs Table 1 placards
It must be carried in a cargo tank
explanation: Column 3 shows the hazard class or division, or the word Forbidden. Never transport a Forbidden material.

prompt: Which column of the Hazardous Materials Table lists the identification number?
choices: Column 2
Column 4
Column 3
Column 6
explanation: Column 4 lists the identification number for each proper shipping name. Column 2 has the shipping names, Column 3 the hazard class, and Column 6 the required labels.

prompt: In Column 7 of the Hazardous Materials Table, what do the special provision numbers 1 through 6 tell you?
choices: The packing group is I
The material is a marine pollutant
The material is a poison inhalation hazard
The material is forbidden by air
explanation: Numbers 1-6 in Column 7 mean the material is a poison inhalation hazard (PIH), which has special requirements for shipping papers, marking and placards.

prompt: A material has an (A) in Column 1 and is not a hazardous substance or hazardous waste. It is shipped by truck. Do the HMR apply?
choices: No, the (A) entry applies only to air transport
Yes, every listed material is regulated by highway
Only if the vehicle crosses a state line
Yes, but only if it weighs over 1,001 pounds
explanation: (A) means the material is subject to the HMR only when offered or intended for transport by air, unless it is a hazardous substance or hazardous waste.

prompt: Which columns of the Hazardous Materials Table do NOT apply to highway transportation?
choices: Columns 1 and 2
Columns 7 and 8
Columns 5 and 6
Columns 9 and 10
explanation: The manual notes that Columns 9 and 10 of the Hazardous Materials Table do not apply to transportation by highway. Columns 1-8 (symbols, names, class, ID number, packing group, labels, special provisions, packaging) do.

prompt: An identification number begins with "NA" rather than "UN." What does that tell you?
choices: The material is a marine pollutant
The shipping name is used only within the U.S. and to and from Canada
The material is not regulated by highway
The material is for international air shipment
explanation: NA numbers go with proper shipping names used only within the United States and to and from Canada. ID numbers relate to air shipments under ICAO rules.

prompt: A bulk package of a marine pollutant is being hauled. Which is true about the MARINE POLLUTANT mark?
choices: It replaces the hazard class placard on the vehicle
It is only required when the load travels by water
It is only noted on the shipping paper, not on the package
It is a marking, not a placard, and must also be shown on the vehicle
explanation: Bulk packages of a marine pollutant must show the MARINE POLLUTANT marking, which is not a placard, and it must also be displayed on the outside of the vehicle. The shipping paper must say "Marine Pollutant."

prompt: How large must a hazmat placard be?
choices: At least 100 mm (3.9 inches) square
At least 15 inches square
At least 250 mm (9.84 inches) square, set on point
At least 6 inches square
explanation: Placards are at least 250 mm (9.84 inches) square, square-on-point in a diamond shape. The 100 mm (3.9 inch) size is for ID numbers on bulk packaging.

prompt: When must placards be attached to a vehicle that requires them?
choices: Before you drive it
Within 24 hours of loading
Only before crossing a state line
Before you enter a city
explanation: Attach placards before you drive. You may move an improperly placarded vehicle only in an emergency to protect life or property.

prompt: Which of these placard practices is prohibited?
choices: Displaying a placard when not required, if it shows the actual hazard
Placing the front placard on the trailer
Mounting placards on a contrasting background
Showing a "Drive Safely" slogan with the placards
explanation: Slogans such as "Drive Safely" are prohibited. The front placard may be on the tractor or trailer, placards must be on a contrasting background, and placards may be shown even when not required as long as they identify the hazard.

prompt: To decide which placards you need, which three things must you know?
choices: The hazard class, the amount shipped, and the total weight of all hazmat on board
The vehicle's CDL class, the type of packaging used, and the length of the trailer
The shipper's name, the receiver's name, and the carrier's name
The route, the weather, and the delivery time
explanation: To choose placards you need the materials' hazard class, the amount shipped, and the total weight of all classes of hazardous materials in your vehicle.

prompt: Which of these requires placards in any amount?
choices: Class 8 corrosives
Division 1.1 explosives
Class 3 flammable liquids
Division 2.2 non-flammable gases
explanation: Placard Table 1 materials, including Divisions 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 explosives, must be placarded whenever any amount is transported. Classes 3, 8 and 2.2 are Table 2 materials.

prompt: You are hauling 100 pounds of Division 4.3 (dangerous when wet) material in non-bulk packages. Is a placard required?
choices: Yes, but a DANGEROUS placard is used instead
No, but you must carry the ERG
Yes, a DANGEROUS WHEN WET placard, because it is a Table 1 material
No, only loads of 1,001 pounds or more need placards
explanation: Division 4.3 is a Placard Table 1 material, so it must be placarded DANGEROUS WHEN WET in any amount.

prompt: Your only cargo is 800 pounds of Class 8 corrosives in non-bulk packages. What placards are required?
choices: DANGEROUS placards
CORROSIVE placards
CORROSIVE placards on the front and rear only
None
explanation: Class 8 is a Table 2 material. Except for bulk packaging, Table 2 materials need placards only when the total is 1,001 pounds or more.

prompt: Your non-bulk load is 600 pounds of Class 3 flammable liquid and 500 pounds of Class 8 corrosive from one shipper. What placards may you use?
choices: FLAMMABLE placards only
FLAMMABLE and CORROSIVE placards, or DANGEROUS placards instead
None, because each class is under 1,001 pounds
DANGEROUS placards only; class placards are not allowed
explanation: Add all Table 2 amounts: 1,100 pounds is 1,001 or more, so placards are needed. With two Table 2 classes and less than 2,205 pounds of either loaded at one place, DANGEROUS may replace the separate placards, but it is optional.

prompt: You load 2,500 pounds of Class 8 corrosive at one shipper and 1,200 pounds of Class 3 flammable liquid at another. Can DANGEROUS placards cover the Class 8?
choices: No, the whole load needs a Table 1 placard
Yes, DANGEROUS may cover any mix of Table 2 classes
No, the Class 8 must have CORROSIVE placards
Yes, if the trip is under 100 miles
explanation: When 2,205 pounds or more of one Table 2 class is loaded at one place, you must use the specific placard for that material. DANGEROUS could still be used for the Class 3.

prompt: A shipping paper says INHALATION HAZARD for a small package. What placarding is required?
choices: POISON INHALATION HAZARD or POISON GAS placards, plus class placards, in any amount
Only a DANGEROUS placard, because the package is small
Only the hazard class placard, once the load reaches 1,001 pounds
No placards, because the total is under 1,001 pounds
explanation: If INHALATION HAZARD appears on the shipping paper or package, display the POISON GAS or POISON INHALATION HAZARD placard in addition to other required placards. The 1,000-pound exception does not apply.

prompt: A material has a secondary hazard of dangerous when wet. When must the DANGEROUS WHEN WET placard be displayed?
choices: Only when the material weighs 1,001 pounds or more in total
Only when it is raining or snowing
Never; only the primary hazard is placarded
In any amount, in addition to the other required placards
explanation: Materials with a secondary hazard of dangerous when wet must display DANGEROUS WHEN WET placards in addition to other placards. The 1,000-pound exception does not apply.

prompt: You are hauling 3,000 pounds of Class 9 miscellaneous hazardous material within the United States. Is a Class 9 placard required?
choices: Only if the vehicle has a cargo tank
Yes, a DANGEROUS placard is required
No, it is not required for domestic transportation
Yes, because the total weight is 1,001 pounds or more
explanation: Class 9 is in Placard Table 2, but the Class 9 placard is not required for domestic transportation.

prompt: Packages bearing which radioactive label require placards in any amount?
choices: Radioactive Yellow III
Radioactive Yellow II
Radioactive White I or Yellow II
Radioactive White I
explanation: Class 7 materials with the Radioactive Yellow III label are in Placard Table 1, so any amount must be placarded RADIOACTIVE.

prompt: What is bulk packaging?
choices: Any container holding a liquid
A single container with a capacity greater than 119 gallons
Any shipment of hazardous materials weighing more than 1,001 pounds
Several drums strapped together
explanation: Bulk packaging is a single container with a capacity greater than 119 gallons.

prompt: A cargo tank has just been unloaded but still holds the residue of a hazardous material. Must it stay placarded?
choices: Only for Table 1 materials
Yes, bulk packages must be placarded even with only residue
Only if the residue is over 119 gallons
No, placards come off as soon as it is unloaded
explanation: A bulk package, and a vehicle transporting it, must be placarded even if it holds only the residue of a hazardous material.

prompt: What should you do first, before loading or unloading hazardous materials?
choices: Turn on the four-way flashers and set out reflective triangles
Remove the placards
Open all the trailer vents
Set the parking brake so the vehicle will not move
explanation: Before loading or unloading, set the parking brake and make sure the vehicle will not move.

prompt: Which tool should never be used when loading hazmat packages?
choices: Hooks
Hand trucks
Pallet jacks
Loading ramps
explanation: Do not use any tool that might damage containers or packaging during loading. Do not use hooks.

prompt: When loading or unloading, the manual lists classes you must never smoke around. Which of these is on that list?
choices: Division 2.2 (Non-flammable gases)
Class 9 (Miscellaneous)
Class 5 (Oxidizers)
Class 8 (Corrosives)
explanation: Never smoke around Class 1 explosives, Division 2.1 flammable gas, Class 3 flammable liquids, Class 4 flammable solids, or Class 5 oxidizers.

prompt: Partway through a trip you notice a package has shifted. Which action is allowed in transit?
choices: Emptying the package into a drum
Re-securing the package so it cannot move
Moving some product into a sturdier package
Opening the package to check the contents
explanation: All hazmat packages must be secured. After loading, do not open any package during the trip and never transfer hazmat from one package to another in transit. A cargo tank may be emptied, but no other package.

prompt: Cargo heater rules usually forbid using a cargo heater with which group of materials?
choices: Class 6, Class 7, and Class 8
Division 2.2, Class 8, and Class 9
Class 4, Class 5, and Class 6
Class 1, Division 2.1, and Class 3
explanation: Special cargo heater rules apply to Class 1 explosives, Division 2.1 flammable gas and Class 3 flammable liquids. Unless you have read all the rules, don't load them in a space with a heater.

prompt: You are hauling Class 4 flammable solids on a flatbed. When may they be carried outside a closed cargo space?
choices: Only when the weather is dry and no rain is forecast
Whenever the total load is under 1,001 pounds
Only if all packages are fire and water resistant, or under a fire and water resistant tarp
Only if the packages are strapped down and it is daylight
explanation: Class 1, Class 4 and Class 5 cannot be overhang or tailgate loads. They must be in a closed cargo space unless all packages are fire and water resistant or covered with a fire and water resistant tarp.

prompt: A floor liner is required for Division 1.1, 1.2 or 1.3 explosives. Which liner is acceptable?
choices: A non-metallic liner or one made of non-ferrous metal
A galvanized steel liner
A stainless steel liner, because it will not rust or spark
A cast iron plate
explanation: The liner must be non-metallic or non-ferrous metal (metal that contains no iron). Stainless and galvanized steel both contain iron, so they are not acceptable.

prompt: When may a Division 1.1, 1.2 or 1.3 explosive be transferred from one vehicle to another on a public roadway?
choices: Only in an emergency, with warning devices set out
Whenever the receiving vehicle is placarded
Only at night
Whenever traffic is light and the shoulder is wide enough
explanation: Do not transfer these explosives on a public roadway except in an emergency. If safety requires it, set out red warning reflectors, flags or electric lanterns.

prompt: A package of explosives shows an oily stain. What should you do?
choices: Load it in a separate corner
Refuse to take the package
Load it if the label is readable
Wipe it clean and load it
explanation: Never transport damaged packages of explosives. Do not take a package that shows any dampness or oily stain.

prompt: May you haul Division 1.1 explosives in a combination that includes a placarded cargo tank?
choices: Yes, if the tank holds a non-flammable liquid
Yes, if the trip is under 50 miles
No, this is not allowed
Yes, if both units are placarded
explanation: Do not transport Division 1.1 or 1.2 in a vehicle combination if there is a marked or placarded cargo tank in the combination.

prompt: Where may nitric acid be placed in a mixed load?
choices: Only next to oxidizers
Only on top of other cargo
Anywhere, if it is in a carboy
Never above any other product
explanation: Do not load nitric acid above any other product.

prompt: Corrosive liquids must never be loaded next to or above which of these?
choices: Division 4.1 flammable solids
Class 9 miscellaneous materials
Division 2.2 non-flammable gases
Non-hazardous dry goods
explanation: Never load corrosive liquids next to or above Division 1.4 explosives, Division 4.1, Division 4.3, Class 5 oxidizers, or Division 2.3 Zone B poisonous gases.

prompt: Where must a package labeled POISON never be loaded?
choices: In a trailer with a sealed floor
Behind other cargo
In a closed van
In the driver's cab or sleeper
explanation: Never load a POISON or POISON INHALATION HAZARD package in the driver's cab or sleeper, or with food for human or animal consumption.

prompt: A load includes Division 6.1 poison that is not overpacked in an approved way. Which item may NOT go in the same vehicle?
choices: Jars of skin cream
Bagged animal feed
Cases of mouthwash
Boxes of toothpaste
explanation: Poisons may not be loaded with human or animal food unless overpacked in an approved way. Foodstuffs are things you swallow; mouthwash, toothpaste and skin creams are not foodstuffs.

prompt: What is the maximum total transport index of all radioactive packages in a single vehicle?
explanation: The transport index tells the degree of control needed in transport. The total transport index of all packages in a single vehicle must not exceed 50.

prompt: Which materials must never be loaded with cyanides or cyanide mixtures?
choices: Non-flammable gases such as nitrogen and helium
Class 7 radioactive materials
Class 9 materials
Acids and other corrosive or acidic materials
explanation: Cyanides must not be loaded with acids, corrosives or other acidic materials that could release hydrocyanic acid.

prompt: What is the difference between a cargo tank and a portable tank?
choices: A cargo tank stays on the vehicle; a portable tank is loaded off the vehicle
A cargo tank is under 119 gallons
A cargo tank holds gases; a portable tank holds liquids
A portable tank cannot be placarded
explanation: Cargo tanks are bulk packaging permanently attached to the vehicle and stay on it during loading and unloading. Portable tanks are loaded or unloaded off the vehicle and then put on it for transport.

prompt: The person watching a cargo tank during loading must be within how many feet of the tank?
choices: 100 feet
25 feet
50 feet
10 feet
explanation: The qualified person attending loading or unloading must be alert, have a clear view of the tank, be within 25 feet, know the hazards and emergency steps, and be authorized and able to move the tank.

prompt: You need to move a cargo tank holding a small amount of hazmat 50 feet across the yard. What about the manholes and valves?
choices: Close only the valves
Leave them open, since a short move inside the yard is allowed
Close them all before moving, no matter how short the distance
Close only the manholes
explanation: Close all manholes and valves before moving a hazmat tank, no matter how small the amount or how short the distance. It is illegal to move it with open valves or covers unless it is empty under 49 CFR 173.29.

prompt: When filling a cargo tank of flammable liquid through an open filling hole, when must the tank be grounded?
choices: Grounding is needed only for compressed gas tanks, not liquids
Only while the pump is running
Only after the filling hole is closed
Before opening the filling hole, until after it is closed
explanation: Ground the tank before opening the filling hole and keep it grounded until after the filling hole is closed.

prompt: Your engine runs the pump while delivering compressed gas. When should you turn the engine off?
choices: After the product transfer, before unhooking the hose
After you drive away from the site
After unhooking the hose, before driving away from the site
Before starting the product transfer
explanation: If you use the engine for transfer, turn it off after product transfer and before you unhook the hose.

prompt: How close to the traveled part of the road may you park with Division 1.1, 1.2 or 1.3 explosives?
choices: Never within 300 feet
Never within 25 feet
Never within 5 feet
Never within 15 feet
explanation: Never park with Division 1.1, 1.2 or 1.3 explosives within five feet of the traveled part of the road.

prompt: Except for brief operational needs like fueling, you may not park a vehicle with Division 1.1 explosives within how many feet of a bridge, tunnel or building?
choices: 100 feet
300 feet
500 feet
200 feet
explanation: Do not park within 300 feet of a bridge, tunnel, building, place where people gather, or open fire, except briefly for necessities such as fueling.

prompt: You are hauling Division 1.2 explosives. Where may you let someone else watch the parked vehicle for you?
choices: In any well-lit rest area
On any private property
At any truck stop with security
On the shipper's, carrier's, or consignee's property
explanation: Someone must always watch the vehicle. You may let someone else watch it only if it is on the shipper's, carrier's or consignee's property.

prompt: What is a safe haven?
choices: A terminal where hazmat may be moved from one vehicle to another vehicle
An approved place for parking unattended vehicles loaded with explosives
A shelter area during a hazmat spill
A rest area for placarded vehicles
explanation: A safe haven is an approved place for parking unattended vehicles loaded with explosives. Local authorities usually designate them.

prompt: You are driving a placarded vehicle with no explosives. When may you park within 5 feet of the traveled part of the road?
choices: Never
Any time, if your flashers are on
Only when your work requires it, and only briefly
Only at night
explanation: A placarded vehicle not carrying explosives may park within five feet of the traveled part of the road only if your work requires it, and only briefly.

prompt: Your co-driver is asleep in the sleeper berth of your parked placarded truck. Is the vehicle attended?
choices: No, an attendant must be awake and not in the sleeper berth
Yes, if the doors are locked
Yes, if the truck is at a truck stop
Yes, any licensed person inside the vehicle counts as the attendant
explanation: The attendant must be in the vehicle, awake and not in the sleeper berth, or within 100 feet with the vehicle in clear view.

prompt: If the person attending a placarded vehicle is outside it, how close must they be?
choices: Within 100 feet, with the vehicle in clear view
Anywhere in the same parking lot
Within 300 feet
Within 25 feet, even if the vehicle is out of view
explanation: An attendant outside the vehicle must be within 100 feet of it and have it within clear view, know the hazards, know what to do in an emergency, and be able to move it.

prompt: Your empty gasoline cargo tank breaks down on the shoulder. Which warning devices may you use?
choices: Any warning device
Flares placed at least 100 feet away
Reflective triangles or red electric lights
Fusees, since the tank is empty and vapor-free
explanation: Never use burning signals such as flares or fuses around a tank used for Class 3 or Division 2.1, whether loaded or empty. Use reflective triangles or red electric lights.

prompt: When driving a placarded vehicle, which places should you avoid when possible?
choices: Rural two-lane roads
Heavily populated areas, tunnels, narrow streets and alleys
Truck routes
Interstate highways
explanation: Whenever placarded, avoid heavily populated areas, crowds, tunnels, narrow streets and alleys, even if other routes are inconvenient, unless there is no other way.

prompt: Who prepares the written route plan for a load of Division 1.1, 1.2 or 1.3 explosives?
choices: The state police, before the trip begins
The shipper, in every case
The consignee who will receive the explosives
The carrier, unless the driver picks up the load away from the employer's terminal
explanation: Carriers prepare the route plan in advance and give the driver a copy. The driver may plan the route if the explosives are picked up somewhere other than the employer's terminal.

prompt: You may not smoke within how many feet of a placarded cargo tank used for Class 3 flammable liquids?
choices: 10 feet
25 feet
100 feet
50 feet
explanation: Do not smoke within 25 feet of a placarded cargo tank used for Class 3 or Division 2.1, or of any vehicle containing Class 1, 3, 4.1, 4.2 or 5 materials.

prompt: What must you do when fueling a vehicle carrying hazardous materials?
choices: Turn off the engine and have someone at the nozzle controlling the flow
Fuel only with the placards covered
Leave the engine running so the air pressure stays high enough for the brakes
Use only the automatic nozzle latch
explanation: Turn off your engine before fueling, and someone must always be at the nozzle controlling fuel flow.

prompt: What fire extinguisher rating is required on the power unit of a placarded vehicle?
choices: 4 B:C or more
5 B:C or more
1 A:5 B:C or more
10 B:C or more
explanation: The power unit of a placarded vehicle must have a fire extinguisher with a UL rating of 10 B:C or more.

prompt: When must you check each tire on a placarded vehicle?
choices: Only at the end of each trip
Only at the start of each day, during the pre-trip inspection
At the start of each trip and each time you park
Every 500 miles
explanation: You must examine each tire at the beginning of each trip and each time the vehicle is parked.

prompt: Before hauling Division 1.1, 1.2 or 1.3 explosives, the carrier must give you which document?
choices: A police escort permit
A copy of the ERG only
A special explosives CDL
A copy of FMCSR Part 397 and written emergency instructions
explanation: The carrier must give each such driver a copy of FMCSR Part 397 and written instructions on what to do if delayed or in an accident. The driver signs a receipt.

prompt: A driver hauling chlorine in a cargo tank must have which equipment?
choices: A survey meter
An approved gas mask and a leak-control kit for the dome cover plate fittings
Grounding cables for every stop
A second 10 B:C fire extinguisher
explanation: A driver transporting chlorine in cargo tanks must have an approved gas mask and an emergency kit for controlling leaks in dome cover plate fittings.

prompt: You must stop before a railroad crossing in which of these vehicles?
choices: A flatbed hauling steel
Any truck over 26,000 pounds
An empty cargo tank last used for hazmat
A van with 300 pounds of unplacarded Class 9 material
explanation: Stop before a crossing if your vehicle is placarded, carries any amount of chlorine, or has cargo tanks used for hazmat, loaded or empty.

prompt: When required to stop at a railroad crossing, how far from the nearest rail must you stop?
choices: 15 to 50 feet
10 to 25 feet
50 to 100 feet
25 to 75 feet
explanation: Stop 15 to 50 feet before the nearest rail. Go only when sure no train is coming and you can clear the tracks without stopping, and don't shift gears while crossing.

prompt: Who publishes the Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG)?
choices: Each state's fire marshal
The Environmental Protection Agency
The U.S. Department of Transportation
Each carrier
explanation: The ERG is a Department of Transportation guidebook for firefighters, police and industry workers.

prompt: The ERG is indexed by:
choices: Proper shipping name and identification number
Placard color and shape
Shipper name, consignee name, and the carrier's name
Truck type and route
explanation: The ERG is indexed by proper shipping name and identification number, which is why those items on the shipping paper must be correct.

prompt: At a hazmat crash scene, where should you keep people?
choices: Next to the vehicle to help
On the downwind shoulder
Close by and downwind
Far away and upwind
explanation: Keep people away from the scene, far away and upwind, warn others of the danger, and call for help.

prompt: You suspect a fire in your cargo. How should you check before opening the trailer doors?
choices: Spray water into the vent first
Feel the doors; if they are hot, keep them closed
Open one door slightly to look
Open them quickly so the heat and smoke can escape
explanation: Feel trailer doors before opening them. If hot, you may have a cargo fire; opening the doors lets in air and may make the fire flare up.

prompt: Should a driver fight a hazardous materials cargo fire?
choices: Yes, using the 10 B:C extinguisher on the power unit
Yes, if the fire is small
No, not without special training and protective gear
Yes, after opening the trailer doors
explanation: Unless you have training and equipment to do so safely, don't fight hazmat fires. You may use the extinguisher to keep a minor truck fire from spreading to the cargo.

prompt: How should you identify hazardous material leaking from your vehicle?
choices: Use the shipping papers, labels or package location
Touch the liquid with a glove
Smell the vapors carefully
Open the damaged package to read the inside label
explanation: Identify leaking material using shipping papers, labels or package location. Never touch it or try to identify it by smell; toxic gases can destroy your sense of smell.

prompt: At a rest area you find hazmat slowly leaking from your truck, and there is no phone. What should you do?
choices: Drive slowly to the nearest truck stop that has a phone to call for help
Park, secure the area, stay there, and send someone for help
Drive back to the shipper
Leave the vehicle and walk to find help
explanation: Never keep driving with hazmat leaking to find a phone or help. Park, secure the area, stay there, and call or send someone for help with written details.

prompt: After a collision involving a vehicle with explosives, what must happen before the vehicles are separated?
choices: The placards must be removed
The explosives must be covered with a tarp
The engine must be restarted
All explosives must be removed and placed at least 200 feet away
explanation: Remove all explosives before separating vehicles in a collision. Place them at least 200 feet from the vehicles and occupied buildings.

prompt: Compressed gas is involved in an accident with your vehicle. Whom must you notify?
choices: The truck's dealer
The receiving customer only
The gas manufacturer's sales office
The shipper
explanation: You must notify the shipper if compressed gas is involved in any accident.

prompt: A package of flammable solids in your load is smoldering. What should you NOT do?
choices: Remove it from the vehicle if safe
Open the package
Remove unbroken packages to cut fire risk
Warn others of the fire hazard
explanation: Do not open smoldering packages of flammable solids. Remove them from the vehicle if you can safely do so, and warn others of the fire hazard.

prompt: After a spill of radioactive material, when may the vehicle be used again?
choices: As soon as the spill is swept up
After it is aired out with the doors open for 24 hours
After it is cleaned and checked with a survey meter
After the placards are changed
explanation: Do not use the vehicle until it is cleaned and checked with a survey meter. Tell your dispatcher or supervisor as soon as possible.

prompt: Which event requires an immediate phone call to the National Response Center?
choices: A person injured in a hazmat incident needs to be hospitalized
A hazmat delivery is late by a day
A placard falls off during a trip
A package's label is slightly torn
explanation: You or your employer must call when, as a direct result of hazmat, a person is killed, an injured person requires hospitalization, property damage exceeds $50,000, the public is evacuated for more than one hour, a major transportation artery or facility is closed for one hour or more, and in certain other cases.

prompt: A hazmat incident closes a major highway. For how long must it be closed before the National Response Center must be called?
choices: One hour or more
24 hours or more
15 minutes or more
Four hours or more
explanation: An immediate report is required when one or more major transportation arteries or facilities are closed for one hour or more as a direct result of a hazmat incident.

prompt: What is CHEMTREC's main role?
choices: Inspecting cargo tanks
Giving emergency crews technical data on hazardous materials
Collecting incident fines
Issuing hazmat endorsements after the TSA background check
explanation: CHEMTREC has a 24-hour toll-free line and provides emergency personnel with technical information about the physical properties of hazardous materials.

prompt: After a reportable hazmat incident, within how many days must the carrier file a detailed written report?
choices: 90 days
7 days
60 days
30 days
explanation: Carriers must make detailed written reports within 30 days of an incident.

prompt: While you are driving, where must hazmat shipping papers be kept?
choices: In the glove box, so they stay clean and dry
In a pouch on the driver's door, or in clear view within reach while belted
In the sleeper berth, together with your logbook and permits
With the cargo, next to the hazmat packages they describe
explanation: While driving, keep hazmat shipping papers in a pouch on the driver's door, or in clear view within immediate reach while your seat belt is fastened. They must be easy to see for someone entering the cab.

prompt: You leave your placarded truck to eat at a truck stop. Where should the hazmat shipping papers be?
choices: On the driver's seat or in the driver's door pouch
Locked in the glove box
In your pocket, taken with you
Inside the trailer with the cargo
explanation: When you are out of the vehicle, leave the shipping papers on the driver's seat or in the driver's door pouch so responders can find them. You keep them with you only at a crash or incident scene, to hand to emergency personnel.

prompt: How many placards must a placarded vehicle display, and where?
choices: Two, one on the front and one on the rear of the vehicle
At least four identical placards: front, rear, and both sides
Two, one on each side where other drivers can see them
One on the rear, facing following traffic
explanation: A placarded vehicle must have at least four identical placards, on the front, rear, and both sides, so they can be read from all four directions. The front placard may be on the tractor or the trailer.

prompt: How must the identification number of the contents be displayed on a cargo tank?
choices: Only on the shipping paper kept in the cab
In white numbers on a red panel on the rear only
In black numbers on an orange panel, a placard, or a white diamond
On a small label near the tank's outlet valve
explanation: Cargo tanks and other bulk packaging must show the ID number in black 100 mm (3.9 inch) numbers on orange panels, on placards, or on a white diamond-shaped background if no placards are required.

prompt: Your vehicle has no racks for compressed gas cylinders. How must the cylinders be loaded?
choices: Lying down, wedged tightly against each other
On a flat floor, held upright or in boxes that keep them from tipping
Stacked in layers with moving blankets between each layer
Standing loose, so the valves are easy to reach and check
explanation: Without racks, the cargo floor must be flat and cylinders must be held upright, in racks attached to the vehicle, or in boxes that keep them from turning over. A cylinder may lie down only if it is designed so the relief valve is in the vapor space.

prompt: What must you do with the engine before loading or unloading any explosives?
choices: Keep it idling so air pressure stays up
Turn it off, then check the cargo space
Run it only if the cargo heater is needed
Leave it running so you can move quickly in an emergency
explanation: Turn your engine off before loading or unloading any explosives, then check the cargo space: disable cargo heaters and look for sharp points that could damage the cargo.
